body.statement: Let \(K\geq3\), \(m\geq3\), \(1\leq i\leq m-1\), and \(2i\neq m\). For \(C=((m-i)e_0+ie_L,\ ie_0+(m-i)e_L)\) and \(C'=C^\top\), one has \(d(C,C')=3\).
body.justification: This proves that the cubic endpoint gadget is not an artifact of the construction: three heterogeneous units are necessary in general.
body.gap: Neither exact binary test inversion in \cite{RigdonHudgens2015} nor generic group testing in \cite{HemerikGoeman2018} studies the sparse legal-schedule certificate number.
body.consumer: The result bounds the smallest adversarial schedule that a software unit test must include to audit the proposed symmetry classifier.
body.proof_tex:
Put \(j=m-i\).  The stated profiles have endpoint coordinates
\[
 h_0=j,\quad h_L=i,\qquad g_0=i,\quad g_L=j,            \tag{1}
\]
and zero interior coordinates.  Since \(1\leq i,j\leq m-1\), they are not the endpoint corners; since \(2i\ne m\), they are distinct transposes.  Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) therefore makes them inequivalent and gives \(d(C,C')\leq3\).  We prove the reverse inequality.

Fix any \(R\in\mathcal R_0(n,K)\) with \(q(R)\leq2\).  If \(q(R)=0\), the table is diagonal.  If its diagonal histogram is not \(m e_0+m e_L\), both profiles in (1) have zero count; if it is that histogram, Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\) and binomial symmetry give
\[
 W_R(C)=\binom mj\binom mi=W_R(C').                     \tag{2}
\]
The case \(q(R)=1\) is impossible: all diagonal units have zero effect, while the sole heterogeneous unit would have a nonzero effect, contradicting Assumption \(\mathrm{ass{:}weak\text{-}null}\).

It remains to treat \(q(R)=2\).  Label the two heterogeneous units \((a,b)\) and \((c,d)\).  The weak null says
\[
 a+c=b+d.                                                \tag{3}
\]
If a diagonal filler unit has an interior outcome, both endpoint-only profiles have count zero.  We may therefore suppose that every diagonal filler unit is at \(0\) or \(L\).  Expand the assignment count according to which of the two special units are treated.  If an observed special outcome is interior, its contribution is zero for both profiles.  For the remaining possibilities we compare the contributions term by term.

If both special units are treated, their observed outcomes are \(a,c\in\{0,L\}\).  They cannot both be zero, because (3) and nonnegativity would force \(b=d=0\), making both units diagonal.  They cannot both be \(L\), because (3) and the upper bound \(b,d\leq L\) would force \(b=d=L\).  Thus their observed multiset is \(\{0,L\}\).  A nonzero contribution then requires \(m-1\) diagonal fillers at each endpoint, and the two profile coefficients are
\[
 \binom{m-1}{j-1}\binom{m-1}{i-1}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \binom{m-1}{i-1}\binom{m-1}{j-1},                     \tag{4}
\]
which agree.  If both special units are controlled, the identical argument applied to \(b,d\) gives the equal coefficients
\[
 \binom{m-1}{j}\binom{m-1}{i}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \binom{m-1}{i}\binom{m-1}{j}.                         \tag{5}
\]

Finally suppose exactly one special unit is treated.  For definiteness, let the observed outcomes be \(a\) from the first unit and \(d\) from the second.  If \(a,d\in\{0,L\}\) are different, then (3) forces the unobserved outcomes to be the same respective endpoints: for \((a,d)=(0,L)\), one has \(c-b=L\), hence \((c,b)=(L,0)\), and both response types are diagonal; the reverse case is symmetric.  This contradicts their designation as heterogeneous.  Therefore the two observed outcomes equal some \(v\in\{0,L\}\).  Equation (3) then gives \(b=c\), so the special response types have the form \((v,u)\) and \((u,v)\) with \(u\ne v\).  One observation of \(v\) lies in each arm.  A nonzero contribution requires \(m-2\) diagonal fillers at \(v\) and \(m\) at the other endpoint \(\bar v=L-v\).  Its coefficients for \(C\) and \(C'\) are
\[
 \binom{m-2}{h_v-1}\binom m{h_{\bar v}}
 \quad\hbox{and}\quad
 \binom{m-2}{g_v-1}\binom m{g_{\bar v}}.              \tag{6}
\]
They agree because (1) gives \(h_v+g_v=m\) and \(h_{\bar v}+g_{\bar v}=m\), so each binomial coefficient in (6) equals its complementary coefficient.  The other split allocation is identical with the two labels exchanged.

The four allocations of the special units exhaust Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}assignment\text{-}count}\).  Equations (4)--(6) therefore imply \(W_R(C)=W_R(C')\) for every legal \(R\) with \(q(R)\leq2\).  Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}randomization\text{-}kernel}\) gives the same equality for probabilities, so Definition \(\mathrm{def{:}separator\text{-}size}\) yields \(d(C,C')\geq3\).  Together with the upper bound, this proves \(d(C,C')=3\).

For the requested smallest-instance audit, take \(K=3\), \(m=3\), \(L=2\), and \(i=1\).  Formula (9) in the proof of Theorem \(\mathrm{thm{:}alphabet\text{-}frontier}\) becomes
\[
 R=E_{20}+2E_{01}+E_{00}+2E_{22}.
\]
Both potential-outcome totals are \(6\), and direct expansion over its \(\binom63=20\) balanced assignments gives counts \(1\) for \(C=((2,0,1),(1,0,2))\) and \(0\) for \(C'\).  Independently enumerating the nonnegative \(3\times3\) integer tables of mass \(6\), imposing the weak-null equation and \(q(R)\leq2\), leaves \(103\) tables; the exhaustive allocation argument above gives equal counts for every one of them.  Thus the cubic witness passes the finite early-kill check without the check being used as a premise of the general proof.
